extracted.intended_audience: DEA registrants and applicants for DEA registration, and their legal counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Administrative decision setting out the legal and procedural standards the Drug Enforcement Administration applies when denying (or revoking/suspending) a DEA certificate of registration, including default procedures, statutory bases, burden allocation, and factors considered in determining whether an applicant can be entrusted with registration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory basis for denial/revocation based on exclusion (21 U.S.C. 824(a)(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursuant to 21 U.S.C. 824(a)(5), the Attorney General is authorized to suspend or revoke a registration upon finding that the registrant "has been excluded (or directed to be excluded) from participation in a program pursuant to section 1320a-7(a) of Title 42." The Agency may also deny an application upon finding that an applicant has been excluded from a federal health care program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites precedent where the Agency consistently holds exclusion under 42 U.S.C. 1320a-7(a) supports denial (e.g., Mark Agresti, Samirkumar Shah, Arvinder Singh). The Agency has held exclusion can be a basis to deny even if the underlying conviction is not related to controlled substances (collecting cases; e.g., Phong H. Tran).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory exclusion under 42 U.S.C. 1320a-7(a) as dispositive evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A mandatory exclusion from participation in Medicare, Medicaid, and all federal health care programs under 42 U.S.C. 1320a-7(a) constitutes substantial record evidence supporting denial of a DEA registration application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example factual posture: HHS/OIG exclusion effective date and exclusion period (the decision cites an 11-year mandatory exclusion). The presence of such an exclusion establishes a prima facie case for denial under 21 U.S.C. 824(a)(5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to request a hearing results in default and admission of factual allegations (21 CFR 1301.43)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant fails to file a written request for a hearing, the applicant is deemed to have waived the right to a hearing and be in default; a default "shall be deemed to constitute a waiver of the registrant's right to a hearing and an admission of the factual allegations of the [OSC]."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory citations: 21 CFR 1301.43(e). In default, the Government may file a request for final agency action with a supporting record, and the Administrator may enter a default final order (21 CFR 1301.43(f)(1); 1316.67). The decision notes the applicant did not request a hearing or move to excuse the default.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie burden on Government; burden shifts to applicant to show trustworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Government meets its prima facie burden of showing the application should be denied (e.g., by proving exclusion), the burden shifts to the applicant to show why he/she/they can be entrusted with a registration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites case law describing burden-shifting (Morall v. DEA, Jones Total Health Care Pharmacy v. DEA) and agency practice. The Agency found that substantial record evidence established the Government's prima facie case in this matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust determination is fact-dependent and considers multiple factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The issue of whether a registrant can be entrusted with a DEA registration is inherently fact-dependent and must be assessed based on the individual registrant's circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Agency looks to a range of factors (see related criteria) and applies precedent (Jeffrey Stein, Jones Total Health Care Pharmacy). The decision emphasizes individualized assessment rather than categorical rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registrant's acceptance of responsibility (unequivocal acceptance required)
rubrics_metrics.description: A registrant who committed acts inconsistent with the public interest must accept responsibility for those acts and demonstrate that he/she will not engage in future misconduct; the Agency requires an unequivocal acceptance of responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites precedent requiring unequivocal acceptance (Janet S. Pettyjohn, Mohammed Asgar) and notes that absence of any representations or admissions weighs against the registrant. Failure to accept responsibility supports denial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candor during investigation and hearing as an important factor
rubrics_metrics.description: The registrant's candor during the investigation and any hearing is an important factor in determining acceptance of responsibility and the appropriate sanction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Jones Total Health Care Pharmacy and Hoxie v. DEA. Lack of candor or failure to engage weighs against mitigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Past performance as predictor of future conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Past performance is the best predictor of future performance; prior misconduct strongly informs the Agency's assessment of future trustworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Jones Total Health Care Pharmacy and ALRA Labs as authority for relying on past conduct to assess future risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Egregiousness and extent of misconduct influence sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: The egregiousness and extent of a registrant's misconduct are significant factors in determining the appropriate sanction (e.g., denial, suspension, revocation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Jones Total Health Care Pharmacy (noting egregiousness and extent matter) and other precedent; more severe or extensive misconduct supports more severe sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need to deter similar acts (general and specific deterrence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Agency considers the need to deter similar acts by the individual registrant and by the community of registrants when determining the appropriate sanction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Jeffrey Stein v. DEA for deterrence considerations; deterrence objectives may support denial even where other mitigating factors are present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy of service and due process: "reasonably calculated" notice (Jones v. Flowers; Mullane)
rubrics_metrics.description: Service of process and notice must be reasonably calculated, under all the circumstances, to apprise the registrant of the pendency of the action; email can satisfy due process where email is not returned undeliverable and other methods have been unsuccessful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Jones v. Flowers, Mullane, and prior agency decisions (Mohammed S. Aljanaby, Emilio Luna) finding email service adequate when delivered and other attempts fail. The decision summarizes the DEA investigator's attempts (email, mail, personal service attempts) and finds due process satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural authority to enter final order on default and to file Request for Final Agency Action
rubrics_metrics.description: In the event of a default, DEA may file a Request for Final Agency Action (RFAA) with a supporting record and the Administrator may enter a default final order pursuant to the cited regulations (e.g., 21 CFR 1301.43(c), (f), 1301.46, 1316.67).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The RFAA may state the Administrator is authorized to render DEA's final order without making findings, but 21 CFR 1316.67 requires the Administrator's final order to set forth findings of fact and conclusions of law (citation and cross-reference to JYA LLC d/b/a Webb's Square Pharmacy decision).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory authority cited for administrative action (21 U.S.C. 823(g)(1), 21 U.S.C. 824, 28 CFR 0.100(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision relies on statutory and regulatory authorities empowering the Administrator and the Department to deny, revoke, or suspend registrations and to issue orders (e.g., 21 U.S.C. 823(g)(1), 21 U.S.C. 824, and delegation statutes like 28 CFR 0.100(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Order invokes these statutes as the legal basis for denying the pending application and for the Administrator's authority to sign and publish the document; administrative signing formalities do not alter legal effect.
